items.title: Find My AI Chips: the US Plans to Track GPUs Abroad - IEEE Spectrum
items.summary: To deduce an AI chip’s location, PLV measures the time it takes for a ping to travel from the chip to multiple trusted “landmark” servers around the world and back. Kyle Miller, a senior research analyst at CSET and coauthor of the report, says that for new AI chips, manufacturers could integrate PLV functionality into the hardware itself, while a firmware update could be applied to chips already in circulation. [...] Not all AI chips should be tracked, the researchers note. “The priority should be for the highest-end data center chips—the cream of the crop in high-end data center GPUs,” says Jacob Feldgoise, a senior data research analyst at CSET and coauthor of the report. [...] Whether or not a “Find My” for AI chips becomes a regulatory requirement, Feldgoise envisions tighter conditions for the export of advanced AI chips. “This is based on the increasing importance of compute to national and economic security,” he says. “The chips that generate compute are being seen as a strategic resource, so I would be unsurprised if the due diligence requirements on these devices increase as time passes.”

items.title: Google's chip business is on a faster track than Nvidia's own AI boom
items.summary:
Google introduced two new tensor processing units, or TPUs — its homegrown AI chips — on Monday. The TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max join the 8t and 8i it unveiled in April, the first time Google has introduced four TPU systems in a single year. Both new chips ship next year. [...] Think of it as a chip menu. The 8tx keeps data encrypted for governments, banks, and other regulated businesses, paired with processors from AMD (AMD). The 8i Max squeezes two chips into one package for requests with long context windows — the amount of information an AI model can juggle at once. [...] Google is selling on price. SemiAnalysis found that Google's current Ironwood TPU delivers up to nearly three times as much AI output per dollar as Nvidia's Blackwell chips when running AI agents, though Nvidia's top system still wins when speed is everything.

items.title: Quantum Error Correction: From Memory to Logic
items.abstract: Quantum computers possess computational power distinct from classical devices, using phase coherence and entanglement. This coherence is fragile and susceptible to environmental noise. Protecting quantum information is a central goal of quantum error correction and fault tolerance, which are essential for scaling quantum devices to utility-scale computation. Such protection, however, often requires a space-time overhead formidable for current experimental platforms. A key question is the minimum space-time cost of protecting a quantum information-processing task and how to attain it. This thesis investigates these questions from quantum memory to logical gates. For quantum memory, we consider preserving information while it idles under noise. We first develop the near-optimal fidelity, an optimization-free general framework that bounds the optimal performance of a given encoding and noise channel and provides an achievable recovery benchmark. We apply it to Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes, which encode information in quantum harmonic oscillators through lattice geometry. We show that finite-size GKP memories can substantially outperform existing recovery schemes. In the asymptotic system size and energy limit, GKP families achieve the capacities of pure-loss and quantum-limited amplification channels, attaining the minimum encoding redundancy permitted by these channels. For logical gates, we study quantum low-density parity-check codes. We introduce high-rate surgery, which performs parallel, addressable logical Pauli-product measurements with low space-time overhead. Our analytical constructions and complementary numerical benchmarks indicate that logical processing can retain nearly constant space-time overhead relative to quantum memory. These results provide efficient building blocks for utility-scale quantum devices.

items.title: Space-bounded quantum state testing via space-efficient quantum singular value transformation
items.abstract: Abstract Driven by exploring the power of quantum computation with a limited number of qubits, we present a novel complete characterization for space-bounded quantum computation, which encompasses settings with one-sided error (unitary ) and two-sided error ( ), approached from a quantum (mixed) state testing perspective: The first family of natural complete problems for unitary $$\text {\textsf {coRQL}} $$ coRQL , namely space-bounded quantum state certification for trace distance and Hilbert–Schmidt distance; A new family of (arguably simpler) natural complete problems for , namely space-bounded quantum state testing for trace distance, Hilbert–Schmidt distance, and (von Neumann) entropy difference. In the space-bounded quantum state testing problem, we consider two logarithmic-qubit quantum circuits (devices) denoted as $$Q_0$$ Q 0 and $$Q_1$$ Q 1 , which prepare quantum states $$\rho _0$$ ρ 0 and $$\rho _1$$ ρ 1 , respectively, with access to their “source code”. Our goal is to decide whether $$\rho _0$$ ρ 0 is $$\epsilon _1$$ ϵ 1 -close to or $$\epsilon _2$$ ϵ 2 -far from $$\rho _1$$ ρ 1 with respect to a specified distance-like measure. Interestingly, unlike time-bounded state testing problems, which exhibit computational hardness depending on the chosen distance-like measure (either -complete or -complete), our results reveal that the space-bounded state testing problems, considering all three measures, are computationally as easy as preparing quantum states. Our results primarily build upon a space-efficient variant of the quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) introduced by Gilyén, Su, Low, and Wiebe (STOC 2019), which is of independent interest. Our technique provides a unified approach for designing space-bounded quantum algorithms. Specifically, we show that implementing QSVT for any bounded polynomial that approximates a piecewise-smooth function incurs only a constant overhead in terms of the space required for (special forms of) the projected unitary encoding.

items.title: Nonreciprocal Relaxation Acceleration
items.abstract: Abstract Driven by recent discoveries regarding the quantum Mpemba effect, the anomalous relaxation dynamics of open quantum systems have garnered significant attention. While expediting thermalization to equilibrium has been extensively studied, dynamically accelerating the convergence toward nonequilibrium steady states remains a formidable challenge. In this letter, we find that a transiently engineered nonreciprocal dissipative channel can provide a shortcut that accelerates relaxation to the target reciprocal nonequilibrium steady state. Using a two-mode interacting bosonic model, we demonstrate that the temporal activation of a nonreciprocal channel effciently suppresses prolonged inter-mode energy oscillations, enforcing a rapid, unidirectional thermal dump into the environment. Counterintuitively, under symmetric local dissipation, both nonreciprocal directions exhibit relaxation speedup with identical asymptotic spectral decay rates. Our results establish a route to accelerated nonequilibrium steady-state preparation in the studied bosonic model, with a covariance-based suffcient condition that extends to a multimode chain.

items.title: Quantum neural networks for wind power prediction: a benchmark against classical machine learning models
items.abstract: Abstract Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is an emerging field at the intersection of quantum computing and machine learning that aims to enhance classical learning methods by leveraging principles such as superposition and entanglement. However, skepticism remains regarding its practical advantages, particularly due to the limitations of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. This study addresses these concerns through a systematic evaluation of Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs), quantum-inspired counterparts of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). We construct and analyze 12 distinct QNN configurations by combining two quantum feature maps with six entanglement strategies for ansatz design. Experiments conducted on a wind energy dataset show that QNNs can achieve competitive or superior performance compared to classical baseline models, with the best-performing configuration (QNN-3) reaching an R 2 score of up to 0.94 when forecasting wind power output using four input features. In addition, we provide a detailed analysis of simulation time across different configurations, highlighting trade-offs between model complexity and computational cost. These findings demonstrate the potential of QNNs as viable models for predictive tasks and contribute to the ongoing evaluation of QML in real-world applications.
